# Coordinate systems {#sec-m2-crs}

This is the shortest chapter and the one that prevents the most errors. Almost every problem of "the layers don't
overlap", "the area came out wrong" or "the *buffer* turned oval" is a projection problem.

```{r}
library(sf)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

# default basemap for mapview(): OpenStreetMap
mapview::mapviewOptions(basemaps = c("OpenStreetMap", "Esri.WorldGrayCanvas", "Esri.WorldImagery"))
```

## The two types of system

**Geographic** (degrees): latitude and longitude coordinates on an ellipsoid. Good for
storing and exchanging data; bad for measuring.

**Projected** (metres): the curved surface flattened onto a plane. Good for measuring distances,
areas and making *buffers*; it introduces a distortion that grows with the size of the area.

```{r}
#| echo: false
crs_relevantes <- data.frame(
  epsg = c(4326, 4674, 31982, 31983, 31984, 5880),
  name = c("WGS 84", "SIRGAS 2000", "SIRGAS 2000 / UTM 22S", "SIRGAS 2000 / UTM 23S",
           "SIRGAS 2000 / UTM 24S", "SIRGAS 2000 / Brazil Polyconic"),
  type = c("geographic", "geographic", "projected", "projected", "projected", "projected"),
  use = c("GPS, OSM, GTFS, international files",
          "official Brazilian standard (IBGE, DNIT)",
          "PR, SC, western SP",
          "SP, RJ, MG, GO",
          "CE, BA, PE (Fortaleza)",
          "maps of the whole of Brazil")
)
knitr::kable(crs_relevantes)
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Which one to use in the Ministry

- To **store and distribute** data: SIRGAS 2000 (`EPSG:4674`). It is Brazil's official geodetic
  system. Data from GPS, OSM or GTFS arrive in WGS 84 (`EPSG:4326`); in
  practice the difference between the two is a few centimetres, but declare the right one.
- To **measure** at a local or regional scale: the corresponding UTM zone.
- For **national maps**: the Brazil Polyconic (`EPSG:5880`) or an equal-area projection
  (Albers), defined below.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Where to look up an EPSG that is not in this table

<https://epsg.io/> accepts searches by place name, code or keyword, and shows the area of
use, the unit and the code ready to paste (`EPSG:xxxx`). `sf` also exposes the same database
locally, without needing the internet:

```{r}
#| eval: false
sf::st_crs("EPSG:31982")            # full details of a known code
sf::st_crs(32722)                   # also accepts the bare number
```
:::

## Query, set and transform

These are three different operations, and confusing them is the most common error.

```{r}
portos <- data.frame(
  nome = c("Paranaguá", "Itajaí"),
  lon  = c(-48.5119, -48.6486),
  lat  = c(-25.5016, -26.9077)
) |>
  sf::st_as_sf(coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4326)

# 1. QUERY: what is the CRS?
sf::st_crs(portos)$input
sf::st_crs(portos)$epsg
```

```{r}
# 2. SET: state the CRS of data that came without this information.
#    It does NOT move the coordinates, it only labels them.
sem_crs <- sf::st_set_crs(portos, NA)
sf::st_crs(sem_crs)$input

corrigido <- sf::st_set_crs(sem_crs, 4326)
sf::st_crs(corrigido)$epsg
```

```{r}
# 3. TRANSFORM: convert the coordinates to another system.
#    It MOVES the coordinates, recomputing them.
portos_utm <- sf::st_transform(portos, 31982)
sf::st_crs(portos_utm)$epsg
sf::st_coordinates(portos_utm)
```

Compare the coordinates: in UTM they are metres from the zone's central meridian, in the
hundreds of thousands. In degrees they were numbers between -49 and -25.

::: {.callout-important}
## `st_set_crs()` never fixes a wrong overlay

If two layers do not line up, the wrong reflex is `st_set_crs()`. It only swaps the label and
leaves the coordinates in the wrong place. The right one is `st_transform()`. Use `st_set_crs()`
**only** when the data arrived without a CRS and you know, from the documentation, what it is.
:::

## When reprojecting is mandatory

```{r}
# distance between two ports, in geographic coordinates
sf::st_distance(portos[1, ], portos[2, ])
```

Modern `sf` uses the `s2` library and computes correct **geodesic** distances even in
degrees. For distance, you no longer need to reproject.

With *buffers* the story is more delicate. On projected data, `dist` is in the CRS unit
(metres, in UTM). On geographic coordinates, `sf` also accepts metres, because it delegates to
`s2`. The result, however, is an **approximation by spherical cells**, slower and less
predictable at the edges:

```{r}
b_graus  <- sf::st_buffer(portos[1, ], dist = 10000)                    # via s2, in metres
b_metros <- portos[1, ] |> sf::st_transform(31982) |> sf::st_buffer(10000)  # planar, in metres

c(
  s2_km2  = as.numeric(units::set_units(sf::st_area(b_graus),  km^2)),
  utm_km2 = as.numeric(units::set_units(sf::st_area(b_metros), km^2))
)
```

A 10 km *buffer* should have an area close to π × 10² ≈ 314 km². Always check with this mental
arithmetic: it is the quickest check that the projection was right. Looking at it
helps to see the difference between the two approaches:

```{r}
mapview::mapview(b_graus, col.regions = "#1a5b8a") +
  mapview::mapview(b_metros, col.regions = "#b3402a")
```

The classic problem appears when `s2` is switched off, in old versions of `sf` and in
many other programs: the radius is interpreted **in degrees**, producing a "buffer" thousands
of kilometres wide.

```{r}
sf::sf_use_s2(FALSE)
b_errado <- suppressWarnings(sf::st_buffer(portos[1, ], dist = 10000))
sf::st_bbox(b_errado)          # the bounding box goes beyond the planet
sf::sf_use_s2(TRUE)            # always switch it back on
```

That is why the recommendation for metric work stays the same: **reproject to UTM, do the
operations, and go back to 4674 when writing the result**. That way the code works the same in
any version and can be audited by whoever opens it in QGIS.

The rule of thumb:

| Operation | Need to reproject? |
|:--|:--|
| `st_distance()` | no (`s2` handles it in degrees) |
| `st_buffer()` | **yes**: the radius is in the CRS unit |
| `st_area()`, `st_length()` | no for global values, **yes** for local precision |
| `st_intersection()`, `st_join()` | no, but the layers must be in the **same** CRS |
| regular grids, *snapping*, routing | **yes** |

## Layers in different CRSs

```{r}
#| error: true
# two layers in different systems: the operation fails (and it is good that it does)
sf::st_intersects(portos, sf::st_transform(portos, 31982))
```

The pattern to align everything to a working CRS:

```{r}
#| eval: false
crs_trabalho <- 31982

camadas <- list(rodovias = rodovias, setores = setores, portos = portos)
camadas <- lapply(camadas, st_transform, crs = crs_trabalho)
```

A useful function to find the right UTM zone from the data itself:

```{r}
zona_utm <- function(x) {
  centro <- suppressWarnings(sf::st_centroid(sf::st_as_sfc(sf::st_bbox(sf::st_transform(x, 4326)))))
  lon <- sf::st_coordinates(centro)[1]
  lat <- sf::st_coordinates(centro)[2]
  zona <- floor((lon + 180) / 6) + 1
  # SIRGAS 2000 / UTM: 31978+zone-17 in the southern hemisphere (zones 18S to 25S)
  epsg <- if (lat < 0) 31960 + zona else 31954 + zona
  epsg
}

zona_utm(portos)          # PR/SC -> 31982 (UTM 22S)
```

For maps and calculations covering the whole of Brazil, the equal-area projection used by IBGE and
Ipea:

```{r}
crs_brasil <- paste("+proj=aea +lat_0=-12 +lon_0=-54 +lat_1=-2 +lat_2=-22",
                    "+x_0=0 +y_0=0 +ellps=GRS80 +units=m +no_defs")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-crs-comparacao
#| fig-cap: "The same state in three projections: geographic, UTM 22S and Brazil Albers"
#| fig-height: 3.2
arquivo <- "dados/brutos/pr.gpkg"
if (!file.exists(arquivo)) {
  pr <- geobr::read_state(code_state = "PR", year = 2020, showProgress = FALSE)
  sf::st_write(pr, arquivo, quiet = TRUE)
}
pr <- sf::st_read(arquivo, quiet = TRUE)

mapa <- function(x, titulo) {
  ggplot(x) + geom_sf(fill = "#d7e3ee", colour = "#1a5b8a", linewidth = 0.3) +
    labs(title = titulo) + theme_void(base_size = 9) +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5))
}

patchwork::wrap_plots(
  mapa(sf::st_transform(pr, 4674),       "SIRGAS 2000 (degrees)"),
  mapa(sf::st_transform(pr, 31982),      "UTM 22S (metres)"),
  mapa(sf::st_transform(pr, crs_brasil), "Brazil Albers"),
  nrow = 1
)
```

All three are the same geometry. The difference in shape is each projection's distortion. And that is
why the choice matters when the result is going to be measured, not just looked at.
